heartbreak.label: Separation and heartbreak
heartbreak.insight: Feelings of love are no shame. The Prophet ﷺ felt for Mughith, who walked behind Barirah weeping, and he interceded for him — then respected her decision when she refused. The Quran sets the manners of separation: “retain her according to acceptable terms or release her with good treatment,” and “do not forget graciousness between you.” Whoever leaves something for Allah's sake, Allah replaces it with something better; and “perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you.”

now: Allow yourself to grieve without despising yourself or the other person
Reduce the triggers: do not watch their accounts and do not reread old messages
week: Fill your time with good company and physical activity
Pour out your pain to Allah in prostration, and ask Him to compensate you
long: Learn from the experience without punishing yourself
Do not enter a new relationship just to forget the old one
If divorce and rights are involved, consult a religious and a legal professional

questions: What have I learned about myself from this relationship?
Is what I miss the person themself, or the feeling of security?
avoid: Pursuing the other person after they have said no
Revenge or exposing them
Clinging to an unlawful relationship

marriage_seek.label: Marriage and choosing a spouse
marriage_seek.insight: In the Sunnah, marriage is built first on “religion and character” (“choose the one who is religious”; “when someone whose religion and character you are pleased with proposes to you, marry him”), without ignoring other considerations. Whoever seeks marriage intending chastity has Allah's help. And whoever's marriage is delayed finds a path and a hope in “let those who do not find the means to marry keep themselves chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty,” and a door in the prayer of Musa: “My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need.”

now: Pray istikharah if you have a specific choice in front of you
Write down your essential criteria (religion, character, compatibility) and separate them from the extras
week: Ask people who know the suitor (or the woman proposed) closely
Talk calmly with your family about your criteria and theirs
long: Use the waiting time to develop yourself and your relationship with Allah
Seek forgiveness often and pray with certainty, without impatience

questions: What am I really looking for in a life partner?
Is my refusal, or my family's, based on religion and character, or on secondary considerations?
avoid: Clinging to an unlawful relationship while waiting to marry
Despairing and blaming fate
Agreeing under pressure without being convinced

parenting.label: Raising children
parenting.insight: Prophetic upbringing rests on mercy (“He is not one of us who does not show mercy to our young”), gentleness (“kindness is not found in anything except that it beautifies it”), example before instruction (“protect yourselves and your families” — it begins with oneself), fairness between children (“fear Allah and be just between your children”), and long patience (“and be steadfast therein”). Anas served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years and he never once asked him “why did you do that?” And when a young man openly confessed his desire, he did not rebuke him but said “come close” and reasoned with him.

now: Take a breath before you respond; do not punish while angry
Describe the behaviour, not the person: “this action is wrong,” not “you are bad”
week: Spend one-to-one time with your child every day, even 15 minutes, without phones
Reason with them through questions instead of lectures, as the Prophet ﷺ did with the young man
Check yourself: do I do what I ask of them?
long: Be fair between your children in giving and in attention
Pray often for your children and never pray against them
Build a friendship so that your child confides in you before anyone else

questions: Does my child know I love them even while I correct their mistake?
What behaviour do I blame my child for that I do myself?
When did we last talk without orders or blame?
avoid: Hitting or humiliating
Comparing your children with each other or with other people's children
Threats that are never carried out
Praying against your children

parents.label: Honouring and relating to parents
parents.insight: Allah joined kindness to parents with worshipping Him: “And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him, and to parents, good treatment,” singled out their old age, and forbade even saying “uff.” Honouring them does not fall away because of disagreement: “But if they endeavour to make you associate with Me… do not obey them but accompany them in this world with appropriate kindness,” and the Prophet ﷺ told Asma' to keep ties with her polytheist mother. Ibrahim addressed his father who opposed him with “O my father” and “Peace be upon you.” Obedience is in what is right, not in sin or harm.

now: Lower your voice and soften your words in your next conversation with them
Pray for them: “My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small”
week: Do something that makes them happy without them asking
If there is a disagreement, choose a calm time and speak respectfully: “O my father / O my mother”
Ask your siblings to share in caring for them
long: See serving them in old age as an opportunity for Paradise, not a burden
Learn to balance honouring them with your independence in permissible decisions

questions: Do I disagree with them on the substance, or only on the manner?
What do my parents need from me emotionally, not just materially?
avoid: Raising your voice or sighing in annoyance
Cutting ties because of a disagreement
Obeying them in a clear sin or in wronging others

siblings.label: Brothers and sisters
siblings.insight: The story of Yusuf and his brothers is the Quran's greatest proof that jealousy between siblings can reach a terrible point — and that forgiveness is possible even after the worst harm: “No blame will there be upon you today.” The Sunnah warns against the causes of estrangement: “be just between your children,” and “it is not permissible for a Muslim to forsake his brother for more than three days.” And reconciling people is better than the rank of fasting and prayer.

now: Do not answer an offence with a similar offence
If the dispute is about money (inheritance), separate the rights from the feelings
week: Take the first step with a greeting or a friendly message: “the better of the two is the one who greets first”
Ask a trusted elder in the family to help reconcile
long: In inheritance matters, refer to a scholar or a court to determine the rights fairly
Keep the tie of kinship, even at the minimum

questions: What is the real root of the dispute: money? Old favouritism? A hurtful word?
Can I separate my right from my relationship with my brother or sister?
avoid: Long estrangement
Involving the children in the dispute
Giving up your lawful rights under pressure, or taking someone else's

kin.label: Ties of kinship and relatives
kin.insight: The tie of kinship hangs from the Throne, and “the one who maintains ties is not the one who merely reciprocates; rather, the one who maintains ties is the one who keeps them when they are cut.” To the man who kept ties with relatives who cut him off, the Prophet ﷺ said: “You will continue to have a supporter from Allah against them as long as you remain like this.” Abu Bakr resumed spending on his relative who had joined the slander against his daughter, when it was revealed: “Would you not like that Allah should forgive you?” Keeping ties of kinship brings wider provision and a longer legacy.

now: Send a message asking after a relative you have lost touch with
If a relative has hurt you, do not respond by cutting them off completely
week: Choose the lowest possible level of contact and keep to it (a greeting, a call on special occasions)
Give a small gift to a relative who is cold towards you
long: Set boundaries that protect you from harm without cutting the tie
Make keeping ties a regular habit, not a reaction

questions: Am I waiting for them to make the first move?
What is the minimum contact I can keep without being harmed?
avoid: Making contact conditional on being treated the same way
Backbiting at family gatherings
kin.help: If a relative inflicts serious physical or emotional harm, protecting yourself comes first, and keeping the minimum safe contact is enough.

friends.label: Friendship and friends
friends.insight: In the Sunnah, friendship is a life-shaping decision: “A man follows the religion of his close friend, so let each of you consider whom he befriends,” and “the example of a good companion and a bad one is that of one carrying musk and one blowing a blacksmith's bellows.” Disagreements happen even between Abu Bakr and ‘Umar; what matters is reconciling quickly, accepting apologies and preserving the bond of goodwill. Love is declared (“when a man loves his brother, let him tell him”) and nourished with gifts and greetings.

now: If you have fallen out with a friend, send a short message that starts with a greeting
If a friend apologises to you, accept it
week: Evaluate your company: does it bring me closer to Allah or further away?
Tell a good friend how much you love and appreciate them
long: Invest in one deep, righteous friendship
Gradually distance yourself from company that pulls you into wrong

questions: Do my friends make me a better version of myself?
Have I refused an apology I should not have refused?
avoid: Sacrificing your principles to please your friends
Revealing a friend's secrets after a falling-out

betrayal.label: Betrayal and broken trust
betrayal.insight: The Prophetic way with betrayal combines two things: verification and justice in judging (as in the story of Hatib ibn Abi Balta‘ah, when the Prophet ﷺ said “say only good about him” after hearing his excuse), and wisdom in protecting oneself (“a believer is not stung twice from the same hole”). Forgiveness is a virtue, not an obligation, and it does not mean restoring full trust immediately. Yusuf forgave his brothers after years, but only after they had admitted their wrong and their state had changed.

now: Do not make a final decision in the moment of shock
Verify the facts: what do you know for certain?
week: Hear the other person's account if possible, as the Prophet ﷺ heard Hatib
Decide: is this betrayal a passing mistake or a repeated pattern?
Set boundaries that protect you from it happening again
long: Forgiveness can be in the heart while caution remains in your dealings
Rebuild trust gradually if sincere repentance becomes clear
Do not generalise the experience to all people

questions: Am I looking for the truth, or for confirmation of what I feel?
What do I need in order to feel safe again?
Will forgiveness here protect me, or expose me to harm again?
avoid: Taking revenge with a similar betrayal
Judging without verifying
Staying in a harmful relationship in the name of forgiveness

forgive.label: Forgiveness and pardon
forgive.insight: In the Quran, forgiveness is a rank above justice: “The retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation — his reward is with Allah.” Forgiveness does not reduce one's honour but increases it: “Allah increases a servant in honour through forgiveness.” Yet it is a voluntary virtue that the wronged person is never forced into, and the Quran ties it to “makes reconciliation”: praiseworthy forgiveness is the kind that sets things right, not the kind that encourages the wrongdoer to persist. And the greatest motive: “Would you not like that Allah should forgive you?”

now: Separate forgiveness (a decision of the heart) from restoring trust (a gradual process)
Pray: “Our Lord, put not in our hearts resentment”
week: If the wrongdoer apologises, accept the apology even if you have not yet forgotten
Write down what you have lost and what you will gain if you forgive
long: Forgiveness is a journey, not a moment; you may need to renew the decision

questions: Does my not forgiving hurt them, or does it hurt me?
Will forgiveness here set things right, or encourage the harm to be repeated?
avoid: Forgiving in words while continuing to throw the past in their face
Forcing yourself to feel what you do not feel yet
Forgiving ongoing harm without protecting yourself
